questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify what burnishing achieves on gilded leaf
questions.stem: In the log for the restoration of the buffet car, the glazier records that gold leaf was laid on a wet ground and then rubbed with a smooth tool until the leaf shone. What does the burnishing step achieve?

options.text: It presses the leaf onto the ground and brings up its shine, so the surface reads as metal.
It thins the leaf so that a greater area can be covered from a single sheet.
options.misconception: describes burnishing as a way of thinning the leaf

options.text: It removes the gilding so that the paint underneath can be cleaned and repainted.
options.misconception: treats burnishing as a stripping or removal process

options.text: It fixes the leaf so that the wet ground cannot lift it again on the next day.
options.misconception: confuses burnishing with the laying-in of the leaf

questions.explanation: Burnishing compacts the laid leaf and polishes the metal surface until it catches the light. Thinning, stripping and fixing are separate operations and none of them produces the lustre of gold.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the metal surface under the tool.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the light admitted by a set of window panels
questions.stem: The dispatcher's log records that the carriage window glass was cut in four panels to let in as much daylight as possible, and that each panel admits 12 square units of light while the surrounding timber blocks off 4. How many square units of light reach the saloon?

options.text: Twelve square units, since only the largest panel counts toward the light.
options.misconception: counts a single panel instead of the whole set

options.text: Forty-eight square units, since four panels of 12 units each are added together.
Sixty square units, since the 4 units lost to the timber have been added on.
options.misconception: adds the amount blocked by the timber back into the total

options.text: Thirty-two square units, since each panel has been counted as only 8 units of light.
options.misconception: reduces each panel's contribution without any cause

questions.explanation: Four panels each admitting 12 units give 48 units in all, and the 4 units lost to the timber are not added back. The figure records only the light that actually reaches the saloon.
questions.hint: Multiply the units per panel by the number of panels.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a camera obscura projects and what it offers an artist
questions.stem: A dispatcher mentions that the artist working in the booking office once traced a bright patch on the wall. Explain what the camera obscura is and what an artist could take from it.

answer.exemplar: The camera obscura is a dark box with a small opening onto a bright scene, inside which the scene is projected inverted onto a pale surface. An artist could draw the projected image directly, and the device explains the flattened lighting, sharp silhouettes and single consistent source of light that appear in such drawings.

questions.explanation: A darkened box with one opening projects the outside scene, inverted, onto an inner surface. That gives the artist reliable outlines and lighting, though nothing about colour.
questions.hint: Think about a dark room with a small hole in one wall.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the enlarged dimension of a squared-up design
questions.stem: A poster for the new express service is to be squared up from a rough sketch 12 centimetres wide. The sign painter wants the finished width to be 3.5 times the sketch width. What finished width in centimetres should be marked out?
questions.explanation: Squaring up multiplies the small size by the chosen factor, so 12 multiplied by 3.5 gives 42 centimetres. Working from the smaller dimension first keeps the proportions intact across the design.
questions.hint: Multiply the sketch width by the enlargement factor.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the source of an intense blue pigment

stimulus.body: Log entry 14, restoration of the first-class saloon: the paint used for the deep blue of the evening sky was analysed and reported as the naturally occurring stone called lapis, ground to powder and bound in oil. The entry notes that the pigment was bought in quantity and cost more than the gold leaf used in the same carriage.

questions.stem: According to the log entry, where did the deep blue of the evening sky come from?

options.text: From the gold leaf, applied in a thin layer to produce a cool and metallic sheen.
options.misconception: confuses the blue pigment with the gold leaf of the gilding

options.text: From a cheap imitation mixed from other colours so the carriage could be finished in time.
options.misconception: assumes the expensive pigment was replaced by a fake

options.text: From the costly natural stone itself, ground to powder and bound in oil.
From the burnished ground beneath the paint, which gave the sky its depth.
options.misconception: misreads the preparation layer as the source of the colour

questions.explanation: The entry names the natural stone, ground and bound in oil, and prices it above the gold leaf on the same carriage. An imitation or a substitute metal would contradict what was analysed.
questions.hint: Read what the analysis actually reported.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State the effect of tinting a colour with white
questions.stem: On a panel swatch the painter mixes a small amount of blue into white until the blue becomes a pale tint. First name the operation, then state what happens to the colour's value and to its purity.

options.text: Adding a glaze, which keeps the value constant while increasing the depth of the hue.
options.misconception: describes glazing rather than tinting with white

options.text: Mixing with white, which darkens the colour and deepens its saturation.
options.misconception: reverses the effect of white on value and saturation

options.text: Mixing with black, which lightens the tint and increases its transparency.
options.misconception: names the wrong second colour entirely

options.text: Mixing with white, which lightens the colour, raises its value and reduces its purity.

questions.explanation: White adds light, so the tint is lighter and its value rises, while the white itself has no hue, so the blue is diluted and its purity falls. The two effects happen together and pull in opposite directions on colour.
questions.hint: Ask what white contributes to a mixture.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a frame includes and excludes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a frame determines about a picture
questions.stem: The dispatcher's log notes that the picture of the first train through the station was hung in a frame that cropped the sky and part of the platform. What does the frame decide?

options.text: It decides how brightly the picture will appear when lit by the carriage lamps.
options.misconception: treats the frame as a lighting device

options.text: It decides what the viewer is allowed to see, including a scene and excluding the rest of it.
It decides how long the pigments in the picture will remain stable.
options.misconception: credits the frame with protecting the pigments

options.text: It decides the size of the brush used to paint the picture.
options.misconception: imagines the frame dictating the artist's tools

questions.explanation: A frame sets the boundary of the work, so the cropping decides which part of the painted scene the viewer receives. Lighting, pigment stability and the painter's brushes are not decided by a frame.
questions.hint: Ask what the frame cuts away.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate total burnishing time for a gilded panel
questions.stem: The restoration log records that a gilded panel carries 3 square metres of gold leaf and that burnishing took 40 minutes for the first square metre and 25 minutes for each further square metre. How many minutes of burnishing were needed for the whole panel?

options.text: Ninety-five minutes, since the first metre has been counted twice at 40 minutes.
options.misconception: double counts the first square metre in the total

options.text: Seventy-five minutes, since 3 square metres multiplied by 25 minutes gives 75.
options.misconception: ignores the slower rate on the first square metre

options.text: Ninety minutes, since 40 plus two lots of 25 gives 40 plus 50.
Sixty minutes, since the two further square metres have been paid at half the rate.
options.misconception: invents a reduced rate for the later square metres

questions.explanation: The first square metre takes 40 minutes and the remaining two take 25 each, which is 50, so the whole panel took 90 minutes. The first metre is slower because the burnisher is still bedding the leaf down.
questions.hint: Pay the first metre at its own rate, then the rest.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an image made of light is
questions.stem: A colleague asks why some paintings of the goods yard glow so brightly and seem to have no solid body of paint at all. Explain what is meant by an image made of light.

answer.exemplar: An image made of light is built from light itself rather than from opaque pigment: the artist works with thin translucent glazes, reflective grounds and varnishes that return the light to the eye. Because the picture behaves like a surface catching light rather than like a wall covered in colour, it appears to glow, shift with the hour and carry an unusual depth.

questions.explanation: Such a picture returns and transmits the light that reaches it, so it behaves like a surface catching light rather than a surface covered in colour. That is what produces the glow and the sense of depth.
questions.hint: Think about how the surface responds to light.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the magnification of a projected image
questions.stem: A dispatcher keeps a camera obscura box in the signal cabin. Its opening is 5 centimetres wide and the projected image on the pale screen measures 40 centimetres across. How many times wider than the opening is the projected image?
questions.explanation: The projected image is 40 centimetres across and the opening 5, so the image is 40 divided by 5, which is 8 times the width of the opening. The ratio is set by the distance between the opening and the screen.
questions.hint: Divide the width of the image by the width of the opening.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how squaring up preserves a design's proportions

stimulus.body: Log entry 27, carriage poster: the design was drawn small on a sheet 8 centimetres by 5.6 centimetres, and the finished poster was to be 6 times that size on the platform wall. The painter was told to mark out the enlargement by squaring the small sheet up before drawing on the wall.

questions.stem: According to the log entry, what does squaring the small sheet up achieve?

options.text: It enlarges only the height, so the poster may be stretched taller than the sketch.
options.misconception: assumes the two dimensions are scaled separately

options.text: It copies the sketch exactly, so the finished poster is the same size as the drawing.
options.misconception: confuses squaring up with making a same-size copy

options.text: It transfers the design by tracing, so the small drawing is not needed at all.
options.misconception: mistakes the procedure for simple tracing

options.text: It multiplies both sides by the same factor, so the proportions of the sketch survive.

questions.explanation: Squaring up applies one factor to both dimensions, so a sheet 8 by 5.6 becomes 48 by 33.6 centimetres with its proportions intact. Tracing or stretching only one side would not enlarge the design at all.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to each of the two dimensions.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the costliest pigment was used for the sky
questions.stem: The log notes that the sky was painted with a costly blue stone powder while the hills below were painted with a blue made by mixing cheaper colours. First say why the painter used the expensive stone for the sky, then say what that choice tells the viewer.

options.text: The stone is easier to apply than the mixture, and it tells the viewer the sky was painted last.
options.misconception: reverses the reason for the choice and invents a chronology

options.text: The stone gives an intense, stable blue no cheap mixture can match, and it marks the sky as the finest element.
The stone was cheaper than the mixture, and it tells the viewer the hills are of less importance.
options.misconception: reverses the relative cost of the two blues

options.text: The stone was used because the panel stands outdoors, and it tells the viewer the scene is outdoors.
options.misconception: links the pigment to the setting rather than to its value

questions.explanation: The natural stone yields a depth and stability of blue that a mixture of cheap pigments cannot, so it was reserved for the part of the scene seen most closely. The choice also tells the viewer that the sky is the treasure of the picture.
questions.hint: Ask what the painter could not make any other way.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a tint is lighter but less intense
questions.stem: Why does adding white to a blue make it lighter but also less intense?

options.text: White cools the blue, so the change is one of temperature rather than of lightness.
options.misconception: mistakes a change of value for a change of temperature

options.text: White adds pigment only, so the colour rises in value without losing any of its intensity.
options.misconception: claims tinting adds no dilution of the hue

options.text: White adds light to the mixture, raising its value, and adds no hue, which dilutes its purity.
White strengthens the blue by increasing the amount of pigment held on the surface.
options.misconception: claims white increases the pigment content of a tint

questions.explanation: Two separate things happen: more light comes back from the mixture, and less of the original hue survives in it. That is why every tint is both lighter and less saturated than the colour it was made from.
questions.hint: Ask what white adds and what it takes away.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a frame includes and excludes
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the visible width left inside a frame
questions.stem: The log for the dining car records that a framed view of the harbour was 60 centimetres wide, that 18 centimetres of the painting fell outside the frame rebate on each side, and that 12 centimetres were cut from the top. How many centimetres of painted width actually remain visible?

options.text: Twelve centimetres, since the crop from the top has been counted as the visible width.
options.misconception: reports the top crop as the visible width

options.text: Forty-two centimetres, since only one rebate of 18 centimetres has been subtracted.
options.misconception: removes only one of the two side rebates

options.text: Thirty centimetres, since the 12 centimetres cut from the top have been taken off the width.
options.misconception: takes the top crop off the width instead of the height

options.text: Twenty-four centimetres, since 60 minus two lots of 18 leaves 24.

questions.explanation: Each side loses 18 centimetres, so 36 centimetres of width are excluded, leaving 60 minus 36, which is 24 centimetres. The 12 centimetres cut from the top reduces the height and leaves the width alone.
questions.hint: Both side rebates must come off the width.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how gilding and burnishing work together
questions.stem: A junior in the workshop asks why the gilder lays gold leaf on a wet ground rather than sticking it onto a dry surface. Explain the working of gilding and the part burnishing plays.

answer.exemplar: Gold leaf is laid on a sticky ground, usually gesso with oil or water, that is applied to the object and allowed to become tacky. The leaf is then laid onto that ground and pressed with a cotton pad, and burnishing with a smooth tool brings up the metallic lustre by compacting the leaf. The result is a surface that behaves like a sheet of metal rather than like paint.

questions.explanation: The leaf has no adhesive of its own, so it needs a tacky ground to hold it and a pad to press it flat. Burnishing then compacts and polishes the metal so that it catches light as a sheet of metal would.
questions.hint: Think about how the leaf is held on at all.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage reduction in a thinned wash
questions.stem: The dispatcher records that a glazing solution thins a pigment wash from 100 units of volume to 60 units of volume after adding oil. By what percentage has the volume of the wash been reduced?
questions.explanation: The wash loses 100 minus 60, which is 40 units of volume, and 40 over 100 is 0.4, that is 40 per cent. A thinner wash spreads further and lets more light pass through the layers beneath.
questions.hint: Find the loss, then divide by the original volume.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a camera obscura from a log description

stimulus.body: Log entry 9, the signal cabin: a dark chamber has been fitted above the desk with a small opening facing the yard. On a bright afternoon the shape of the signal post and the chimney beyond it appears on the pale inner wall, turned upside down, and the dispatcher has been asked to keep the shutter closed whenever the yard is in shadow.

questions.stem: What device does the log entry describe?

options.text: A magic lantern, casting a picture from a painted slide onto the inner wall.
options.misconception: confuses a receiving device with a projecting lantern

options.text: A camera obscura, projecting an inverted image of the yard onto the pale inner wall.
A mirror tunnel, reflecting the yard into the cabin without any inversion.
options.misconception: denies the inversion that proves the projection

options.text: A lens camera, taking a picture that is being developed on the pale wall.
options.misconception: misreads the inverted image as a photograph being developed

questions.explanation: A darkened chamber, a small opening and an inverted image on a pale wall are the defining signs of a camera obscura. A lantern would need a slide to project, and a camera would record an image rather than throw it on a wall.
questions.hint: Note the darkness, the small opening and the inversion.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Apply one enlargement factor to both dimensions
questions.stem: A poster design is drawn 6 centimetres tall and is to be squared up by a factor of 5 for the platform wall. First state what the multiplication gives, then say why the same factor must be used for the width.

options.text: It gives a height of 11 centimetres, and one factor must be used on both sides to keep the proportions.
options.misconception: subtracts the factor instead of multiplying by it

options.text: It gives a height of 30 centimetres, and the width may be scaled freely since posters are not measured.
options.misconception: keeps the arithmetic but frees the width from proportion

options.text: It gives a height of 30 centimetres, and one factor must be used on both sides to keep the proportions.
It gives a height of 30 centimetres, and the factor must be inverted so the design grows the other way.
options.misconception: reverses the direction in which the enlargement is applied

questions.explanation: Squaring up is 6 multiplied by 5, which is 30 centimetres of height, and the width must take the same factor so that nothing is stretched. Scaling each side independently would change the proportions of the drawing.
questions.hint: Multiply, then ask why both sides take the same number.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the natural blue stone was prized
questions.stem: Why was the naturally occurring blue stone so prized by painters of the period compared with a blue mixed from cheaper materials?

options.text: The stone was so light in weight that it was used to fill hollow sections of a panel.
options.misconception: mistakes the pigment for a structural filler

options.text: The stone could be bought in bulk, so a whole carriage could be covered with it at once.
options.misconception: claims the stone was cheap and available in bulk

options.text: The stone could be painted over mistakes, hiding any error in the earlier layers.
options.misconception: gives the pigment an unrelated covering use

options.text: Ground stone yields a deep, intense and stable blue that no mixture of cheap pigments can match.

questions.explanation: The natural stone gave a depth, purity and permanence of blue that mixtures of cheaper materials could not approach, which is why it was bought at great cost. Bulk buying, covering mistakes and filling hollows are not properties of the pigment.
questions.hint: Ask what the stone does that a mixture cannot do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compute the strength of a tint from the mixture ratio
questions.stem: The log records a tint test in which 1 part of blue mixed with 3 parts of white gave a tint of one quarter the intensity of the pure blue. What fraction of the original intensity is expected from 1 part of blue mixed with 7 parts of white, on the same rule?

options.text: One half, since each addition of white is taken to halve the tint.
options.misconception: assumes every addition of white halves the strength

options.text: One eighth, since 1 part of blue in 8 parts of mixture gives a share of 0.125.
One quarter, since the blue's share of the mixture does not change with more white.
options.misconception: believes the extra white makes no difference at all

options.text: One sixteenth, since the tint has been halved twice over when the white was doubled.
options.misconception: compounds the loss instead of recomputing the share

questions.explanation: The rule is that a tint equals the blue's share of the whole mixture: 1 in 4 gives one quarter, and 1 in 8 gives one eighth, that is 0.125. More white always dilutes the mixture further.
questions.hint: Express the blue as a share of the whole mixture.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a frame includes and excludes
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a frame shapes the act of looking
questions.stem: A colleague asks why the dispatcher chose a frame that cuts off the platform roof. Explain what a frame does to the act of looking at a picture.

answer.exemplar: The frame is a boundary that decides what counts as the work. By cropping the roof the painter or patron keeps only the portion of the scene that carries the intended subject, and everything beyond the rebate is treated as outside the picture altogether. The viewer is therefore directed to one reading of the scene and is denied the surrounding detail that might open other readings.

questions.explanation: Cropping selects one portion of the painted world and rules out the rest, so the frame narrows the readings a viewer can take. The frame is a statement about what the picture is, not a neutral surround.
questions.hint: Think about what the frame excludes as much as what it shows.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many squares a sheet of leaf will yield
questions.stem: A gilded letter for the station name is cut from a sheet of gold leaf 20 centimetres by 30 centimetres. If the sheet is cut into squares of 4 centimetres a side, how many whole squares can be cut from it?
questions.explanation: The 20 centimetre side yields 5 squares and the 30 centimetre side yields 7 whole squares with 2 centimetres left over, so 5 times 7 is 35 squares. Offcuts cannot be joined to make another square of that size.
questions.hint: Count the squares along each side before multiplying.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a light-based construction from a log description

stimulus.body: Log entry 31, the saloon ceiling: the painters have worked over a bright ground in thin layers, and the log records that the surface takes the light differently at dawn and at dusk, and that the scholars who examined it found the picture was in fact a layer of colour that returns the light.

questions.stem: What does the log entry tell us about how the saloon ceiling was constructed?

options.text: It is a mirror set into the ceiling, so it simply reflects the passengers below it.
options.misconception: confuses a reflective layer with a mirror fitted into the panel

options.text: It is built of opaque paint applied thickly over a dark ground, as panels usually are.
options.misconception: reverses the finding that the layers are thin rather than thick

options.text: It is built of layers that reflect and transmit light, rather than of opaque paint alone.
It is a lamp behind a translucent panel, so it shines with its own light.
options.misconception: mistakes reflected light for light emitted by the picture

questions.explanation: A bright ground worked over in thin layers that returns light and changes with the hour is a construction based on light. A mirror set into the ceiling would reflect the passengers, and a lamp would emit rather than return light.
questions.hint: Weigh up what the entry says about thickness and reflection.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what produces an inverted projected image
questions.stem: The dispatcher's box throws an inverted picture of the yard onto its pale screen. First say what produces the inverted image, then say what an artist would take from that image.

options.text: The bright yard bleeds through the wall, and an artist would take the sound of the yard from it.
options.misconception: invents a physical leak and an entirely irrelevant sound

options.text: A mirror in the box turns the image upside down, and an artist would take its colours from it.
options.misconception: locates the reversal in a mirror and claims it yields colour

options.text: The screen itself reverses the image, and an artist would take the finished composition unchanged.
options.misconception: blames the screen for the inversion and offers a whole composition

options.text: A lens in the opening projects the yard onto the screen and turns it upside down, and an artist could trace its outlines.

questions.explanation: A lens in the opening inverts and projects the scene onto the pale screen, giving the artist accurate outlines and shadows. The projection carries no colour, so it supplies form and light rather than a finished picture.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the box inverts what the eye sees.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Define the procedure of squaring up a design
questions.stem: What does it mean to square up a small drawing so that it can be painted at a larger size?

options.text: To copy it in every detail at the same size, so the large version needs no enlargement.
options.misconception: confuses squaring up with making a same-size copy

options.text: To enlarge it by a fixed factor, multiplying both dimensions so the proportions are kept.
To redraw it freehand from memory, correcting anything that looks wrong in the small version.
options.misconception: describes an improvised redraw rather than a scaled transfer

options.text: To divide it into squares so that the large version can be laid out on a grid.
options.misconception: confuses the procedure with a transfer grid

questions.explanation: Squaring up is a single enlargement applied to both dimensions, so the small drawing's proportions carry over to the large surface. Copying, redrawing from memory and gridding are all different operations.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the two dimensions of the drawing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total cost of a quantity of pigment
questions.stem: The log records that the pigment for the eastbound saloon was 10 units of lapis powder bought at a cost of 6 units per unit. What was the total cost in units of the pigment used on that saloon?

options.text: Six units, since the cost of one unit has been reported as the total.
options.misconception: reports the unit price rather than the total cost

options.text: Sixteen units, since the quantity and the price have been added together.
options.misconception: adds the price and the quantity instead of multiplying them

options.text: Sixty units, since 10 units of powder at 6 units each gives a total of 60.
Forty units, since the unit price has been multiplied by the number of cars painted.
options.misconception: multiplies by a number of cars that the log never gives

questions.explanation: The cost is the quantity multiplied by the price of each unit, so 10 multiplied by 6 gives 60 units. The log gives no figure for the number of cars, so no further multiplier applies.
questions.hint: Multiply the quantity by the price of one unit.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Separate the value and purity changes in a tint
questions.stem: A trainee asks why a blue mixed with a little white looks washed out even though it is clearly lighter. Explain the two separate changes that mixing with white produces.

answer.exemplar: Mixing with white does two things at once. It adds reflected light to the mixture, which raises the value and makes the colour look paler, and it adds a colour that has no hue of its own, which dilutes the blue and lowers its purity and saturation. A tint is therefore lighter and less intense at the same time, and the two changes are independent of one another.

questions.explanation: Lightness comes from added reflected light and loss of intensity comes from dilution by a colourless white. Because the two effects are separate, a tint can be made at any strength without changing the character of the hue.
questions.hint: Ask separately what white adds and what it replaces.

questions.stem: A framed print in the station master's office measures 80 centimetres by 60 centimetres, and the frame covers 5 centimetres along each of the four edges. What is the visible area of the print in square centimetres?
questions.explanation: Each dimension loses 5 centimetres at both ends, so the visible size is 70 by 50 centimetres, and 70 multiplied by 50 gives an area of 3500 square centimetres. The frame removes 10 centimetres from each side of the print.
questions.hint: Reduce both dimensions before multiplying them together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a standard gilding method from a log description

stimulus.body: Log entry 45, vestibule lettering: the gilder recorded that the gold leaf was laid in overlapping squares on a ground still tacky to the touch, that each square was worked from the centre outwards with a cotton pad, and that the finished letters were rubbed with a smooth agate until they shone.

questions.stem: What method of gilding does the log entry record?

options.text: The letters were cast in metal first and then gilded, which accounts for the smooth edges.
options.misconception: misreads the gilding as a covering applied to cast metal

options.text: The leaf was glued directly to the surface and polished to hide the joins between squares.
options.misconception: describes a glued and polished application instead of gilding

options.text: The leaf was applied dry to a hard surface and burnished afterwards to fix loose corners.
options.misconception: claims the leaf was laid dry on a hard ground

options.text: The standard method: leaf laid on a tacky ground and worked out from the centre, then burnished.

questions.explanation: A tacky ground, overlapping squares worked from the centre and a final rub with an agate are the recognised stages of gilding. Gluing, dry application and casting in metal would each contradict the sequence recorded.
questions.hint: Check the order of the stages in the entry.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a light-based picture changes with the hour
questions.stem: The dispatcher notes that the saloon ceiling changes from gold in the morning to green in the evening. First say what this shift indicates about the picture's construction, then say why it is not a change of paint.

options.text: It indicates that the painter repainted the ceiling each evening in a different colour.
options.misconception: explains the shift as repeated repainting

options.text: It indicates a construction that returns light, since the light striking the picture has changed with the hour.
It indicates that the ceiling has faded unevenly over the years of service.
options.misconception: attributes the change to deterioration of the pigments

options.text: It indicates that the ceiling is lit by coloured lamps on a rotating schedule.
options.misconception: invents a lighting schedule that was never recorded

questions.explanation: A picture built to return light changes as the light falling on it changes, which is exactly what the log records. Repainting, fading and a lamp schedule would each require evidence the entry does not give.
questions.hint: Ask what is different at dawn and at dusk besides the picture.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compare a camera obscura with an ordinary window
questions.stem: How does the dark chamber with a small opening differ from an ordinary window?

options.text: It shows the outside scene upright, as though the viewer were looking through it.
options.misconception: ignores the inversion produced by the projecting lens

options.text: It admits more light into the room than a plain window of the same size.
options.misconception: treats the box as a device for gathering more light

options.text: It excludes stray light and projects a single inverted image of the outside scene onto a pale surface.
It records the outside scene so that the image can be developed later like a photograph.
options.misconception: confuses the projected image with photographic recording

questions.explanation: The dark interior and the single small opening are what let one inverted image form on the pale surface, and the box excludes the mixed light of the room. A window shows the scene upright and a camera records rather than projects.
questions.hint: Ask what the darkness and the small opening make possible.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a squared-up dimension from a given factor
questions.stem: The log for the platform poster records that a sketch 14 centimetres wide is to be squared up so that the finished poster is 2.5 times the width of the sketch, and that the sketch's height of 9.5 centimetres must be scaled by the same amount. What finished height in centimetres should be marked out?

options.text: 2.5 centimetres, since the height has been replaced by the enlargement factor itself.
options.misconception: reports the factor instead of the scaled dimension

options.text: 12 centimetres, since the factor has been subtracted from the sketch height instead of multiplied.
options.misconception: subtracts the factor instead of multiplying the height by it

options.text: 21.5 centimetres, since the two sizes have been added together to find the finished height.
options.misconception: adds the two sizes instead of scaling the height

options.text: 23.75 centimetres, since 9.5 multiplied by 2.5 gives 23.75.

questions.explanation: The height takes the same factor as the width, so 9.5 multiplied by 2.5 gives 23.75 centimetres, matching the 35 centimetre finished width. Scaling the sides differently would distort the design.
questions.hint: Apply the same factor to the height as to the width.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one stone was used at several strengths
questions.stem: The log notes that a single lapis stone was ground for the sky and that the remaining powder was graded into paler grades for the hills. Explain why the same stone was used at different strengths for different parts of the scene.

answer.exemplar: The stone was the most precious and hardest-wearing blue available, and once it had been ground the painter could control the strength of the colour by using less of it and more of the binder, or by mixing it with white. Using the costliest material for the sky and its weaker grades for the hills therefore stretched a scarce, expensive pigment while still giving the picture a range of blues.

questions.explanation: A ground stone can be made into any strength by dilution, so the painter could stretch a scarce and costly material across the whole picture. The sky received the richest grade and the hills the weaker ones.
questions.hint: Think about how the strength of a ground pigment can be controlled.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how much pigment a tint consumes
questions.stem: The paint tin holds 300 millilitres of pure pigment. The painter uses white to make tints, and each tint uses the pigment together with four times as much white as pigment. How many millilitres of pure pigment remain after one such tint is mixed?
questions.explanation: Each tint contains one part pigment to four parts white, so the pigment makes up one fifth of the mixture, and 300 divided by 5 is 60 millilitres. The other 240 millilitres in that tint is white.
questions.hint: Find what share of the mixture the pigment represents.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a frame includes and excludes
questions.learningObjective: Read cropping from a log entry

stimulus.body: Log entry 52, the dining car: the view of the harbour is framed by a narrow gilt moulding, and the log records that the sky above the harbour wall and the passengers boarding the train were painted but cannot be seen, since the moulding covers them.

questions.stem: What does the log entry tell us about the relationship between the frame and the painting?

options.text: The moulding protects the painting from the light of the carriage lamps in the saloon.
options.misconception: treats the frame as a protective fitting

options.text: The moulding crops the painting, so what the viewer sees was decided by the frame and not the painter alone.
The moulding shows that the harbour view was painted after the frame was installed.
options.misconception: reads the frame as evidence about the order of the work

options.text: The moulding confirms that the painting was always intended to be seen complete.
options.misconception: ignores the cropping recorded in the log

questions.explanation: The entry says plainly that parts of the painting are hidden by the moulding, which is cropping, and cropping hands part of the decision about the work to the frame. Protection, chronology and completeness are not what the entry records.
questions.hint: Notice which painted passages the entry says cannot be seen.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify which gilding step produces the shine
questions.stem: The gilder's log records a base coat, a tacky ground, the laying of leaf, and a final rub with a smooth tool. First name the step that produces the shine, then say what the shine tells the viewer about the surface.

options.text: The tacky ground produces the shine, and it tells the viewer the leaf was applied wet.
options.misconception: credits the shine to the preparation layer

options.text: Laying the leaf produces the shine, and it tells the viewer the surface is only a thin film of colour.
options.misconception: credits the shine to laying rather than to burnishing

options.text: Burnishing produces the shine, and it tells the viewer the surface behaves like metal rather than paint.
Burnishing produces the shine, and it tells the viewer the leaf was laid on a hard metal plate.
options.misconception: invents a metal plate beneath the leaf

questions.explanation: The shine comes from the final rub, which compacts and polishes the metal so it catches light. A metallic lustre tells the viewer that the colour lies in a layer of metal rather than in a pigment mixed with binder.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four logged stages is a polish.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a light-based picture from ordinary paint
questions.stem: What distinguishes an image made of light from an ordinary painted surface?

options.text: It must be kept outdoors, since daylight changes its appearance too much.
options.misconception: claims the material change forces outdoor display

options.text: It reflects no light at all, so the picture is visible only in total darkness.
options.misconception: claims such a picture reflects no light

options.text: It is painted with an unusual number of layers, one more than any other picture.
options.misconception: reduces the effect to the number of layers used

options.text: It returns and transmits light, so its appearance shifts with the light falling on it.

questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature is the behaviour of the surface under light, which returns and passes it rather than absorbing it. The number of layers and the place of display are not what makes such a picture work.
questions.hint: Ask what the surface does with the light that reaches it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the size of a projected image from the scale
questions.stem: The log records that the signal cabin's chamber projects the yard onto its screen at one twentieth of the size of the yard itself. If a chimney in the yard stands 12 metres tall, how tall is its image on the pale screen in centimetres?

options.text: Two hundred and forty centimetres, since the size has been multiplied by the scale rather than divided.
options.misconception: multiplies by the reduction factor instead of dividing

options.text: Sixty centimetres, since 12 metres is 1200 centimetres and 1200 divided by 20 is 60.
Twelve centimetres, since only the number of metres has been divided by the scale.
options.misconception: divides the metre figure without converting to centimetres

options.text: Six centimetres, since the reduction has been applied twice to the same figure.
options.misconception: applies the reduction factor a second time

questions.explanation: A chimney of 12 metres is 1200 centimetres, and at one twentieth of the size the projected image is 1200 divided by 20, which is 60 centimetres. The scale of the box sets the size of the whole projection.
questions.hint: Convert to centimetres, then apply the reduction.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of squaring up a design
questions.stem: A colleague asks why a painter works from a small drawing rather than painting straight onto a large panel. Explain what squaring up contributes to a faithful result.

answer.exemplar: Squaring up transfers a small, resolved drawing to a large surface by multiplying both dimensions by one chosen factor, so the finished panel keeps exactly the proportions and the placement of every feature of the original. Because the enlargement happens at one measured scale, the composition is not stretched or crowded, and the painter can concentrate on the paint rather than on the drawing.

questions.explanation: Squaring up fixes one scale for the whole transfer, so proportions and the placement of features survive. Painting straight onto the large panel would leave all of that to be judged and corrected by eye.
questions.hint: Think about what is preserved when one factor is used.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the quantity of pigment left after use
questions.stem: The log records that a sack of lapis powder weighing 200 grams is used to make a deep sky colour, and that the sky of the westbound saloon uses 8 grams of it. How many whole grams of powder are left in the sack?
questions.explanation: The sky uses 8 grams of the 200 gram sack, so 200 minus 8 leaves 192 grams of powder for the remaining work. Because the pigment is measured in whole grams the remainder is exact.
questions.hint: Subtract the amount used from the amount held.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify how a recorded colour was lightened

stimulus.body: Log entry 61, the saloon panel: the painters recorded that a colour noted in the older book as a deep sky blue now appears as a pale blue, and that the log states the tint was produced by adding lead white to the pigment until the mixture could no longer be called the deep blue of the book.

questions.stem: What change does the log entry describe, and what does it do to the colour?

options.text: The colour was lightened with more of the same blue, which raised its value and lowered its purity.
options.misconception: claims the blue was tinted with more of itself

options.text: The colour was lightened with a pale yellow, which raised its value and warmed the hue.
options.misconception: substitutes a yellow tinting colour for white

options.text: The colour was lightened with white, which raised its value and lowered its purity.
The colour was thinned with linseed oil, which raised its value and lowered its purity.
options.misconception: confuses tinting with thinning a wash in oil

questions.explanation: The entry names lead white, which adds light and dilutes the hue, so the recorded deep blue becomes pale and less pure. A yellow or an oil would change the hue differently and the entry does not mention either.
questions.hint: Read which material the log says was added.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a frame includes and excludes
questions.learningObjective: Compare what a frame removes and what it gives
questions.stem: The log records a frame whose rebate hides 10 centimetres of painting along every edge. First say what the viewer loses, then say what the frame gains the viewer.

options.text: The viewer loses the light falling on the picture and gains a clearer sense of its size.
options.misconception: claims the frame removes light from the picture

options.text: The viewer loses the chosen scene itself and gains a clearer view of the whole painted world beyond it.
options.misconception: reverses what is kept and what is cut away

options.text: The viewer loses nothing at all and gains a record of when the picture was made.
options.misconception: denies any cropping at all

options.text: The viewer loses the painted surroundings of the chosen scene and gains a defined work that can be hung and read.

questions.explanation: A rebate that hides 10 centimetres on every edge cuts the painted surroundings away, so the viewer receives one scene rather than a whole field. What the frame adds is a boundary that makes the remainder legible as a single work.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of the painting fall outside the rebate.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why fine tools are used when laying leaf
questions.stem: Why does the gilder use a small brush tip and a fine pad rather than a broad one when laying leaf on the lettering?

options.text: Broad tools cannot hold enough leaf to cover a letter in a single pass.
options.misconception: gives a coverage reason for a fine tip

options.text: The leaf is thinner than tissue paper, so it must be guided precisely to land flat without buckling.
Small tools keep the leaf warm, which stops it from sticking to the cotton pad.
options.misconception: invents a temperature problem with the leaf

options.text: The pad must be exactly as wide as the letter, since a wider pad leaves visible marks.
options.misconception: misdescribes the pad as needing to match the letter

questions.explanation: Gold leaf is extremely thin and easily tears, buckles or folds, so it must be placed and pressed with small precise movements. Coverage, temperature and pad width are not the reasons for a fine tip.
questions.hint: Think about how fragile the leaf is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the light leaving a glazed surface
questions.stem: The log records that a glazes panel is lit at one side by a lamp producing 400 units of light, that the glazed surface returns 55 per cent of the light striking it, and that the paint beneath returns a further 20 per cent of what comes through. How many units of light leave the glazed surface?

options.text: Three hundred units, since 55 per cent and 20 per cent have been added together first.
options.misconception: adds the two percentages before applying them

options.text: Two hundred and twenty units, since the 20 per cent from the paint below has been left out.
options.misconception: omits the contribution from the layer beneath the glaze

options.text: Two hundred and sixty-four units, since 220 from the glaze plus 44 from the paint below.
One hundred and eighty units, since the light has been reduced by both percentages at once.
options.misconception: applies both reductions to the same incoming light

questions.explanation: The glaze returns 0.55 of 400, which is 220 units, and the paint beneath returns 0.2 of that 220, which is 44 units, so 220 plus 44 gives 264 units leaving the surface.
questions.hint: Work through the glaze first, then the layer beneath it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a camera obscura gives and what it withholds
questions.stem: A colleague asks why the projected picture in the signal cabin looks so clear and yet so unlike the yard it shows. Explain what the device does and what it cannot give the painter.

answer.exemplar: The camera obscura gathers light from the whole bright scene through a small opening and projects it inverted onto a pale surface, so the drawing is crisp and every edge is sharp because nothing has been invented. What it cannot give is colour, since the projection carries light of all kinds mixed together, nor any sense of the scene as the painter wishes to see it. The device fixes the lighting and the outlines.

questions.explanation: The clarity comes from the projection, which supplies exact outlines and a single light source. The shortcoming is that colour is mixed together in the light, so the device gives form and light rather than the painted scene itself.
questions.hint: Think about what light of many kinds does when it is mixed.

questions.stem: The log records that the emblem for the carriage side is drawn 5.5 centimetres across and is to be squared up by a factor of 9 for the painted panel. What size in centimetres across should be marked out?
questions.explanation: Squaring up multiplies the measured size by the factor, so 5.5 multiplied by 9 gives 49.5 centimetres across. The same factor must be applied to the height, or the emblem will be stretched.
questions.hint: Multiply the drawn width by the enlargement factor.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the costliest pigment was reserved for the sky

stimulus.body: Log entry 74, the night sky: the log records that the blue of the night sky was laid in as a thick opaque coat, that it was found to be the most costly material on the carriage, and that the painter had been ordered to use the precious stone wherever the sky appeared.

questions.stem: Why was the precious stone used for the sky according to the log entry?

options.text: Because it resisted the damp and salt of the running line better than the other pigments.
options.misconception: invents a durability problem with the other pigments

options.text: Because it was the only pigment that could be laid in a thick opaque coat without cracking.
options.misconception: makes an economic choice sound like a technical necessity

options.text: Because the other areas of the carriage had already been painted and could not be repainted.
options.misconception: gives a reason about the schedule of the work

options.text: Because the depth of its blue could be seen fully there and appreciated, and no other part could carry it.

questions.explanation: The entry places the most costly material where its depth would show most, in the sky, and orders its use wherever the sky appears. Technical cracking, working order and durability would each be reasons the entry does not give.
questions.hint: Ask where the best blue would be seen to best advantage.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish value change from intensity change in a tint
questions.stem: A trainee mixes blue with white until the blue looks pale. First say what has happened to the colour's value, then say what has happened to its intensity.

options.text: Its value has fallen, because the blue is diluted, and its intensity has risen, because white is brighter.
options.misconception: reverses both effects of adding white

options.text: Its value has risen, because more light is returned, and its intensity has fallen, because the blue is diluted.
Its value has risen, because the mixture is lighter, and its intensity has risen as well, because white is a colour.
options.misconception: claims white increases saturation

options.text: Neither value nor intensity has changed, because only the proportion of binder has altered.
options.misconception: denies any change at all in the resulting colour

questions.explanation: White adds reflected light, so the value rises, and it adds a colourless body that dilutes the blue, so the intensity falls. The two changes always occur together when a colour is tinted.
questions.hint: Ask what white adds to the light and to the pigment.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a frame includes and excludes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a frame determines what a picture is
questions.stem: Why is the frame described as deciding what the picture is, rather than merely as a decoration around it?

options.text: Because its shape decides whether the picture is hung on a wall or on a ceiling.
options.misconception: attributes to the frame a decision about where a picture hangs

options.text: Because its materials tell the viewer how much the picture cost to commission.
options.misconception: treats the frame as a record of the commission price

options.text: Because it sets the boundary of the work, and everything outside that boundary is excluded from it.
Because the width of its moulding sets the scale of the figures painted inside it.
options.misconception: claims the frame determines the scale of the painted figures

questions.explanation: A frame draws a boundary around the work, and what falls outside it is treated as outside the picture altogether. Price, hanging position and the scale of the figures are not decided by the frame.
questions.hint: Ask where the frame draws the line.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate total burnishing time from a stepped rate
questions.stem: The restoration log records that a gilded panel carries 5 square metres of gold leaf, that burnishing took 30 minutes for the first square metre and 22 minutes for each further square metre. How many minutes of burnishing were needed for the whole panel?

options.text: Ninety minutes, since the last two square metres have been left out of the count.
options.misconception: omits part of the panel from the total

options.text: One hundred and ten minutes, since 5 square metres multiplied by 22 minutes gives 110.
options.misconception: ignores the separate rate on the first square metre

options.text: One hundred and forty minutes, since the first metre has been paid at 40 minutes.
options.misconception: applies a rate that the log never records

options.text: One hundred and eighteen minutes, since 30 plus four lots of 22 gives 118.

questions.explanation: The first square metre takes 30 minutes and the remaining four take 22 each, which is 88, so 30 plus 88 gives 118 minutes. The first metre takes longer because the burnisher is bedding the first leaf down.
questions.hint: Pay the first metre at its own rate, then the rest.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a light-based picture seems to change as the viewer moves
questions.stem: A colleague asks why a picture made of light seems to change as the passenger walks past it. Explain what the viewer is responding to.

answer.exemplar: The layers of such a picture return the light that reaches them, so the picture changes with the angle and strength of the light falling on it. A passenger walking past the carriage sees the surface at a succession of angles and sees something different each time, which is why the work appears to shift and breathe. The paint has not altered; only the light on it has.

questions.explanation: The viewer's movement changes the angle at which light reaches the surface, and the picture's layers return that light differently each time. The change is in the light, not in the paint or in the subject.
questions.hint: Ask what changes for the viewer as they walk past.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an instruction to square up a sheet

stimulus.body: Log entry 88, the timetable poster: the artist was given a sheet on which the design was drawn at one twelfth of the size it was to appear, and the instruction was to mark the enlargement by squaring the sheet up to the wall before any paint was applied.

questions.stem: What does the instruction in the log entry require of the artist?

options.text: Tracing the design through the small sheet, which copies it without enlarging it.
options.misconception: confuses the enlargement with a tracing transfer

options.text: Multiplying the design by twelve in both directions, so its proportions remain true.
Drawing it freehand at the larger size, which allows the proportions to improve.
options.misconception: treats squaring up as an invitation to improvise

options.text: Dividing the design into a grid of squares, which measures the wall for the painter.
options.misconception: confuses the procedure with setting out a grid

questions.explanation: A sheet drawn at one twelfth of the finished size is enlarged by multiplying both dimensions by twelve, which keeps the design true. Tracing, freehand redrawing and gridding are different procedures with different results.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen to the size of the drawing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Draw conclusions about value from the cost of a pigment
questions.stem: The log records that the blue of the sky cost more than the gold on the same carriage. First say what this tells you about the pigment, then say what it tells you about the scale of the sky in the picture.

options.text: It was difficult to apply, and the sky was painted last on the panel.
options.misconception: turns a statement of cost into one about the order of work

options.text: It was the cheapest material available, and the sky was the least important part of the scene.
options.misconception: reverses both the cost and the value of the sky

options.text: It was the most expensive material available, and the sky was treated as the most valuable part of the scene.
It was rare in the region, and the sky was copied from an older panel.
options.misconception: invents a geographical scarcity and a copy from an older panel

questions.explanation: A pigment that costs more than gold was in the highest category of value, and spending it on the sky tells the viewer that the sky is the treasure of the picture. Nothing in the log concerns application, order or copying.
questions.hint: Ask what a painter does with the most costly material.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the pigment added to make a chalky tint
questions.stem: A painter makes a tint of a blue and the result looks chalky. What has been added to the colour, and what two changes does it bring about?

options.text: A pale grey, which lowers the value while leaving the purity of the colour.
options.misconception: invents a grey pigment and denies any change of purity

options.text: Black, which lowers the value of the colour and reduces its purity.
options.misconception: names black and misstates the effect on value

options.text: Yellow, which lowers the value of the colour and warms the hue of it.
options.misconception: names yellow and misstates the effect on value

options.text: White, which raises the value of the colour and reduces its purity and saturation.

questions.explanation: A chalky, pale tint is made by adding white, and white simultaneously raises the value and dilutes the hue. Black and yellow would darken and shift the colour differently, and a grey pigment is not what is used.
questions.hint: Ask which pigment makes a colour both paler and duller.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a frame includes and excludes
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the visible width after two side rebates
questions.stem: The log records that a framed view of the harbour measured 100 centimetres wide and that the frame rebate covered 12 centimetres of painting at the left edge, 18 at the right edge and 10 at the top. How many centimetres of painted width remain visible in the frame?

options.text: Eighty-eight centimetres, since only the rebate of 12 centimetres has been subtracted.
options.misconception: removes only one of the two side rebates

options.text: Seventy centimetres, since 12 plus 18 comes to 30 and 100 minus 30 is 70.
Ninety centimetres, since the rebate at the top has been taken off the width as well.
options.misconception: takes the top rebate off the width instead of the height

options.text: Forty centimetres, since the three rebates have all been taken off the width.
options.misconception: subtracts the top rebate from the width as well

questions.explanation: The two side rebates remove 12 plus 18, which is 30 centimetres of the 100 centimetre width, leaving 70 centimetres visible. The 10 centimetres cut from the top reduces the height of the picture but not its width.
questions.hint: Only the side rebates affect the width.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why gilded surfaces wear differently from paint
questions.stem: A colleague asks why gilding survives handling better than ordinary paint. Explain what makes the gilded surface behave differently.

answer.exemplar: The gilded surface is not paint at all but a very thin sheet of metal held on a ground by a binder and compacted by burnishing. Because the colour lies in a solid metallic layer rather than in a film of pigment mixed with glue, it does not abrade in the same way and it keeps its shine. It can, however, be scratched through, and that is why the gilders work so carefully at the joins.

questions.explanation: The colour of a gilded surface lies in a solid metal layer rather than in a pigment film, so it abrades differently and keeps its lustre where a paint film would wear and dull. It is still vulnerable to being scratched through.
questions.hint: Ask where the colour actually is in a gilded surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the light reflected by a panel
questions.stem: The log records that a glazes panel reflects 30 per cent of the light falling on it and that a second such panel reflects 45 per cent. If 1000 units of light fall on the two together, how many units leave the first panel?
questions.explanation: The first panel returns 30 per cent of the 1000 units, so 1000 multiplied by 0.30 gives 300 units. The second panel's share of 450 units is separate and does not affect the first.
questions.hint: Multiply the incoming light by the first panel's share.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate evidence that a device projects an inverted image

stimulus.body: Log entry 96, the yard cabin: the log records that the box was darkened so that only the small opening admitted light, that the pale screen was hung opposite the opening at a fixed distance, and that the dispatcher noted that the shadow of the signal post fell on the screen sharply and in colour, although the post itself is painted a dark grey.

questions.stem: What does the evidence recorded in the log entry indicate about the device?

options.text: That the screen is showing a reflection of the yard, since the colour of the post is preserved.
options.misconception: uses the colour of the post to argue for a mirror

options.text: That the box is a photographic camera recording the yard, since the image appears on a pale surface.
options.misconception: confuses a projecting box with a recording camera

options.text: That a lens is projecting the scene onto the screen, since the image is inverted and sharply defined.
That the opening is larger than the objects it projects, since the shadow is so sharp.
options.misconception: reads the sharpness of the image as a fact about the opening

questions.explanation: A darkened box, one small opening and a sharp inverted image on a screen together indicate projection through a lens. A camera would record rather than display, and a mirror would not invert the scene in this way.
questions.hint: Ask what the inversion and the sharpness together tell you.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one factor must be applied to both dimensions
questions.stem: A poster sketch is 10 centimetres wide and is to be squared up by a factor of 8 for the platform wall. First state the finished width in centimetres, then say what would happen if only the width were multiplied.

options.text: The finished width is 2 centimetres, and multiplying the width alone would leave the proportions unchanged.
options.misconception: divides the width by the factor instead of multiplying

options.text: The finished width is 80 centimetres, and multiplying the width alone would improve the proportions of the design.
options.misconception: keeps the arithmetic but praises a distortion

options.text: The finished width is 18 centimetres, and multiplying the width alone would keep the design true to the sketch.
options.misconception: adds the factor to the width instead of multiplying

options.text: The finished width is 80 centimetres, and multiplying the width alone would stretch the design out of proportion.

questions.explanation: Squaring up by a factor of 8 gives a width of 80 centimetres, and the same factor must be applied to the height or the drawing will be stretched. A design squared up unevenly no longer looks like the sketch it came from.
questions.hint: Apply the factor, then think about the untouched side.
